back: Carry blood away from the heart at high pressure. They have thick, muscular, stretchy walls.
Carry blood back to the heart at low pressure. They have thinner walls and valves to stop backflow.
Tiny blood vessels with walls one cell thick, where substances pass between the blood and the body's cells.

front: The four chambers of the heart
back: Two atria at the top (they receive blood) and two ventricles at the bottom (they pump blood out).

front: Why is the left ventricle wall thicker than the right?
back: It pumps blood all around the body, which needs more pressure. The right ventricle only pumps blood to the lungs.
White blood cells fight infection. Platelets help blood to clot.
Dissolved substances such as glucose, carbon dioxide and urea.

front: Four ways alveoli are adapted for gas exchange
back: Huge surface area, walls one cell thick, a moist lining and a rich blood supply.

front: What happens when you breathe in?
back: The diaphragm contracts and flattens and the ribs move up and out, so the chest volume increases and air flows in.
glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy released)
Breathing moves air in and out of the lungs. Respiration is a chemical reaction in cells that releases energy from glucose.
A protein that speeds up a chemical reaction without being used up (a biological catalyst).
Amylase: starch → sugars. Protease: proteins → amino acids. Lipase: fats → fatty acids and glycerol.
It breaks fat into tiny droplets so lipase can digest it faster. It is made by the liver and stored in the gall bladder.
Tiny finger-like folds lining the small intestine. They give a huge surface area for absorbing digested food.
Mechanical: breaking food into smaller pieces (teeth, stomach churning). Chemical: enzymes breaking large molecules into small ones.
Large, insoluble molecules must be broken into small, soluble ones that can be absorbed into the blood.
